sources.citation: Zisberg A, Sinoff G, Gur-Yaish N, Admi H, Shadmi E. In-hospital use of continence aids and new-onset urinary incontinence in adults aged 70 and older. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2011;59(6):1099-104.
sources.design: Prospective cohort study; multivariable logistic regression
sources.population_setting: 352 acute medical inpatients aged 70 and over who were continent before admission, 900-bed teaching hospital, Israel; continence aid use and new incontinence both by patient self-report; outcome at discharge only
sources.tool_used: PubMed get_article_metadata; Scite search_literature (closed access, abstract and introduction only); Undermind read_pdfs failed (PDF not available)
sources.correction_check: PubMed: search of this PMID with retracted publication[pt] OR retraction of publication[pt] returned no record (26 Sep 2026); PubMed searches for published erratum[pt]/erratum/correction notices matching the title found none. Scite (checked before its monthly limit was reached) lists an editorial notice DOI 10.1136/ebn.2011.100180 (Sep 2011) tagged both 'has erratum' and 'comment'; this DOI is in Evidence-Based Nursing and looks like a published commentary on the paper rather than a correction, but it could not be opened or found in PubMed. Recheck before publication.
sources.quality_note: Single hospital, one country, modest sample; exposure and outcome self-reported; confidence intervals wide (catheter OR 1.53 to 11.83). Adjusted for function, cognition, illness severity, age and length of stay, but residual confounding by severity and mobility is likely (sicker, less mobile people are more likely to get pads or catheters). Association only. No follow-up after discharge, so persistence of new incontinence is unknown. Full text not opened, so baseline differences between groups were not checked.

Important conflicting evidence for C12-17: 'change in character of urine' (defined as visible blood, colour change or odour change) was modestly associated with bacteriuria plus pyuria. But bacteriuria plus pyuria is itself not sufficient for a UTI diagnosis, and odour was not analysed separately from colour and visible blood.

Composite outcome dominated by screen-detected bacteriuria (daily cultures, threshold 10^3 cfu/mL); authors state results would not differ much with bacteriuria alone. One specific sheath product in five sizes.

claims.claim: In a prospective cohort of 352 acute medical patients aged 70 and over who were continent before admission, 60 (about 1 in 6) reported new urinary incontinence at discharge.
claims.supporting_passage: "A 900-bed teaching hospital in Israel." "Three hundred fifty-two acute medical patients aged 70 and older who were continent before admission." "The development of new UI was defined as participant report of inability to control voiding at discharge." "Of the 352 participants, 58 (16.5%) used adult diapers, and 27 (7.7%) had a UC during most of the hospital stay. Sixty (17.1%) participants developed new UI at discharge."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 70+ continent before admission, acute medical wards, one Israeli teaching hospital / in-hospital use of pads (adult diapers) or urinary catheter for most of the stay vs self-toileting / self-reported new urinary incontinence / at discharge (no later follow-up)
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 352 people aged 70 and over admitted to an Israeli hospital medical ward, all able to control their bladder before admission, about 1 in 6 (60 people) said at discharge that they could no longer control it.
claims.qualifications: One hospital in Israel; incontinence was self-reported at discharge and not followed up afterwards, so we do not know how many recovered. Say 'said they could no longer control their bladder at discharge'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Other hospital studies (cited in the paper's introduction, not opened) give new incontinence rates of 10% to 21%; do not quote these.

numbers.meaning: participants, aged 70+, continent before admission
reported new urinary incontinence at discharge; denominator 352
used adult pads (diapers) for most of the stay; denominator 352
had a urinary catheter for most of the stay; denominator 352

claims.claim: Pad use for most of the stay was associated with higher odds of new incontinence (adjusted OR 2.62) and catheter use with higher odds again (adjusted OR 4.26), compared with self-toileting; association, not proof of cause.
claims.supporting_passage: "Multivariate analyses modeled the association between use of continence aids (vs self-toileting) and the development of new UI, controlling for baseline functional and cognitive status, disease severity, age, and length of stay." "The odds of developing new UI were 4.26 (95% confidence interval (CI)=1.53-11.83) times higher for UC users and 2.62 (95% CI=1.17-5.87) times higher for adult diaper users than for the self-toileting group, controlling for the above risk factors." "The use of adult diapers and UCs during acute hospitalization is associated with the development of new UI at discharge."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C12-09-a; comparator self-toileting; adjusted odds ratios; at discharge
claims.safe_wording: People who wore pads or had a catheter for most of their stay were more likely to report new incontinence at discharge than people who used the toilet themselves, even after the researchers allowed for age, illness severity, mobility and memory. This shows a link. It does not prove that pads or catheters caused the leaking. (Practitioner version may add: adjusted odds ratios 2.6 for pads and 4.3 for catheters, with wide confidence intervals.)
claims.qualifications: Association only; odds ratios must not be turned into 'X times more likely' or into absolute differences. Confidence intervals are wide (catheter 1.53 to 11.83). The paper's own conclusion uses 'associated'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Residual confounding is likely: sicker, frailer or less mobile people are more likely to be given pads or catheters and more likely to leak (see C12-09-c). Reverse causation is possible (people already starting to leak given pads). Full text not opened, so baseline differences between groups were not checked.

numbers.meaning: odds of new incontinence at discharge, pad users vs self-toileting, adjusted; relative
odds of new incontinence at discharge, catheter users vs self-toileting, adjusted; relative

claims.claim: Sicker, frailer people are more likely to be given pads in hospital, so a link between pads and new incontinence may partly reflect who gets pads.
claims.supporting_passage: Larsen 2023: "Patients identified as severely frail had a higher probability of becoming pad users during hospitalization (Odds Ratio=1.57 (95% Confidence Interval: 1.45-1.71);<.001) compared to non/mild/moderate frail patients. Patients who became pad users during hospitalization had a higher risk of a hospital-acquired urinary tract infection (Odds Ratio=4.28 (95% Confidence Interval: 1.92-9.52);<.001)." Zisberg 2011: "controlling for baseline functional and cognitive status, disease severity, age, and length of stay."
claims.pico_timeframe: Larsen: 1,958 acutely admitted patients aged 65+, Aarhus, Denmark, 2017 to 2019 / severe frailty vs less frail / becoming a pad user during the admission; and pad users vs not / hospital-acquired UTI
claims.safe_wording: Frailer people are more likely to be given pads in hospital (shown in a Danish study of about 2,000 older patients), so part of the link between pads and new leaking may come from who is given pads, not from the pads themselves. The Israeli study tried to allow for this, but no observational study can fully remove it.
claims.qualifications: Larsen is a different population (Denmark) and an observational record review; use it only for the direction of the confounding and, if at all, the separate pad-UTI association (not causal).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that contradicts this caveat.

numbers.meaning: odds of becoming a pad user in hospital, severely frail vs non/mild/moderately frail; relative; do not present to the public
odds of hospital-acquired UTI, patients who became pad users vs not; relative, association only

claims.claim: The CDC catheter guideline says urinary catheters should not be used to manage incontinence and lists using an indwelling catheter as a substitute for nursing care of a person with incontinence as inappropriate.
claims.supporting_passage: "2. Avoid use of urinary catheters in patients and nursing home residents for management of incontinence. (Category IB) (Key Question 1A)" Table 2: "B. Examples of inappropriate uses of indwelling catheters: As a substitute for nursing care of the patient or resident with incontinence ... NOTE. These indications are based primarily on expert consensus."
claims.location: Section II Summary of Recommendations, I.A.2 (p. 321); Table 2 (p. 320)
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospital patients and nursing home residents; guideline recommendation (2009)
claims.safe_wording: US infection control guidance (CDC, 2009) says catheters should not be used to manage incontinence, and lists using a catheter 'as a substitute for nursing care' of someone with incontinence as an inappropriate use.
claims.qualifications: US guideline from 2009; the indications table rests mainly on expert consensus. It covers catheters, not pads.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No guideline statement on pads was opened; any recommendation that pads should not be the default is the post's judgement, to be marked as such.

claims.claim: Continence status recorded in hospital often reflects the products in use rather than the person's usual continence.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not found
claims.safe_wording: Do not state this as a finding. The post may ask a question instead (for example: 'Was this person continent before admission?') without claiming how records are usually kept, or how the label affects discharge or care home referrals.
claims.qualifications: No audit or documentation study was found in this batch.

claims.claim: In a study of 97 recently wet pads from nursing home residents, judging infection by urine odour disagreed with the laboratory result in about one third of cases.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ninety-seven recently wet incontinence pads of residents in six Midwestern nursing homes were evaluated for odor within 1 hour of voiding. These results were compared to microscopy and culture results of clean-catch urine samples from these individuals. Defining a UTI as either bacteriuria or bacteriuria and pyuria, using urine odor to identify a UTI resulted in error in one third of cases. Results of this study indicate smell of urine in incontinence pads may be an absent or misleading symptom for UTIs in elderly nursing home residents."
claims.pico_timeframe: 97 pads from incontinent residents, six US Midwestern nursing homes / odour of wet pad / reference: bacteriuria or bacteriuria plus pyuria on clean-catch urine / single time point
claims.safe_wording: In a small US study of 97 wet pads from nursing home residents, judging by smell got the answer wrong about 1 time in 3 when checked against urine tests.
claims.qualifications: Small (97 pads), 2004, US. The 'right answer' was bacteria in the urine, which many residents have without any infection, so this tests smell against a lab finding, not against true infection. The abstract does not split errors into false alarms and misses.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C12-17-b: a larger study found a modest link between changes in urine colour, smell or visible blood and lab signs of infection.

numbers.meaning: recently wet pads assessed
nursing homes
odour judgement disagreed with the urine test result; denominator 97 pads

claims.claim: Changes in urine colour, smell or visible blood were only modestly linked with laboratory signs of infection in nursing home residents, and those laboratory signs do not by themselves mean infection.
claims.supporting_passage: Definition (Methods, p. 3): "change in character of urine (i.e., gross hematuria, change in color of urine, change in odor of urine)". Abstract: "After 178,914 person-days of follow-up, 228 participants had 399 episodes of clinically suspected UTI with a urinalysis and urine culture performed; 147 episodes (36.8%) had bacteriuria plus pyuria. The clinical features associated with bacteriuria plus pyuria were dysuria (relative risk (RR)=1.58, 95% confidence interval (CI)=1.10-2.03), change in character of urine (RR=1.42, 95% CI=1.07-1.79), and change in mental status (RR=1.38, 95% CI=1.03-1.74)." "Diagnostic uncertainty still remains for the vast majority of residents who meet only one clinical feature." Introduction (p. 2): "Thus, bacteriuria plus pyuria alone are not sufficient to make the diagnosis of UTI in a nursing home resident." Table 3 (p. 14, as read with Undermind): change in character of urine present in 144 of 399 episodes, of which 68 (47.2%) had bacteriuria plus pyuria, vs 79 of 255 (31.0%) without it.
claims.location: Abstract; Methods p. 3; Introduction p. 2; Table 3 p. 14
claims.pico_timeframe: 551 residents of five Connecticut nursing homes followed 1 year; 399 episodes of clinically suspected UTI in non-catheterised residents / nurse-reported change in character of urine (visible blood, colour or odour) / bacteriuria plus pyuria / at time of suspected UTI
claims.safe_wording: In a larger US nursing home study, when staff suspected a urine infection, lab signs of infection were found in about 47 in 100 cases where the urine had changed colour, smell or showed blood, and in about 31 in 100 where it had not. So a change in the urine raised the chance a little. The same lab signs are common in residents with no infection at all.
claims.qualifications: The feature combined visible blood, colour and odour; odour was not analysed alone. Visible blood in the urine is itself a reason to seek advice. Outcome was a lab finding (bacteria plus white cells), not confirmed infection. Only people already suspected of UTI were studied.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: This is the main conflicting evidence: smell or colour changes are not meaningless, just weak. The post should say 'poor guide on its own', not 'irrelevant'.

numbers.meaning: episodes of suspected UTI in 228 residents
episodes with a change in urine character that had bacteriuria plus pyuria
episodes without a change in urine character that had bacteriuria plus pyuria
adjusted relative risk of bacteriuria plus pyuria with a change in urine character; relative

claims.claim: Expert surveillance criteria for care homes note that changes in urine colour or odour often occur with harmless bacteria in the urine and other conditions such as dehydration, and require new urinary symptoms plus a positive culture to count a UTI.
claims.supporting_passage: "Acute change in mental status and change in the character of the urine (eg, change in color or odor) were each independently associated with bacteriuria (≥10^5 colony-forming units [cfu]/mL) plus pyuria (≥10 white blood cells per high-power field) in a prospective study of LTCF residents with clinically suspected UTI; however, these 2 symptoms are frequently demonstrated in the presence of asymptomatic bacteriuria due to other confounding clinical conditions, such as dehydration." "The revised definitions take into account the low probability of UTI in residents without indwelling catheters if localizing symptoms are not present, as well as the need for microbiologic confirmation for diagnosis." Table 5 criteria for residents without a catheter: "a. Acute dysuria or acute pain, swelling, or tenderness of the testes, epididymis, or prostate"; "b. Fever or leukocytosis ... and at least 1 of the following localizing urinary tract subcriteria: i. Acute costovertebral angle pain or tenderness; ii. Suprapubic pain; iii. Gross hematuria; iv. New or marked increase in incontinence; v. New or marked increase in urgency; vi. New or marked increase in frequency"; "c. In the absence of fever or leukocytosis, then 2 or more of the following localizing urinary tract subcriteria". For residents with a catheter: "a. Fever, rigors, or new-onset hypotension, with no alternate site of infection"; "c. New-onset suprapubic pain or costovertebral angle pain or tenderness". Note: "Pyuria does not differentiate symptomatic UTI from asymptomatic bacteriuria." Caveat: "the surveillance definitions presented here may not be adequate for real-time case finding, diagnosis, or clinical decision making (eg, antibiotic initiation)."
claims.location: Urinary Tract Infections section and Guiding Principles (PMC full text); Table 5, p. 17 (Undermind read_pdfs); superscripts restored from PDF
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of long-term care facilities; expert consensus surveillance definitions (2012)
claims.safe_wording: Infection experts writing criteria for care homes say that changes in urine colour or smell often happen without infection, for example when someone is not drinking enough. Their criteria look instead for new urinary symptoms: pain or burning passing urine, new or much worse urgency, frequency or leaking, pain low in the tummy or in the side, visible blood in the urine, or fever with any of these.
claims.qualifications: These are surveillance definitions; the authors say they may not be adequate for clinical decision making such as starting antibiotics. Present them as what points to the urinary tract, not as a treatment rule. Older people with a catheter or who cannot report symptoms need separate judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Juthani-Mehta 2009 (C12-17-b) found a modest association between urine character changes and lab findings.

claims.claim: UK guidance (UKHSA) says cloudy urine and dipstick results should not be used alone to diagnose UTI in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not verbatim from the page): dipsticks become more unreliable with increasing age over 65 years; up to half of older adults, and most with a urinary catheter, will have bacteria present in the bladder/urine without an infection. No wording about cloudy urine was seen.
claims.location: WebSearch result summary; page not opened
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults over 65 in primary care, England
claims.safe_wording: Do not quote or paraphrase UKHSA or name it as saying anything about cloudy or smelly urine. The editor has already dropped the dipstick post (C12-18) for resting on UKHSA pages.
claims.qualifications: search_extract only; not sufficient for an essential claim.

claims.claim: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms are common in care home residents; in trials, antibiotics for them brought no clear benefit in deaths or complications and more side effects.
claims.supporting_passage: Krzyzaniak 2022 abstract: "Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is common among residents of residential aged care facilities (RACFs)." "Nine randomised controlled trials, comprising 1391 participants were included; two of which used a placebo comparator, and the remaining seven used no therapy control groups. There was a relatively small number of studies assessed per outcome and an overall moderate risk of bias. Outcomes related to mortality, development of ASB, and complications were comparable between the two groups. Antibiotic therapy was associated with a higher number of adverse effects (four studies; 303 participants; risk ratio [RR] 5.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.07 to 29.55,= 0.04) and bacteriological cure (nine studies; 888 participants; RR 1.89, 95% CI = 1.08 to 3.32,= 0.03)." "The harms and lack of clinical benefit of antibiotic use for older patients in RACFs may outweigh the benefits." Full text (results): "Only Nicolle 1987 reported a breakdown of the types of adverse events experienced by participants. For the antibiotic group, these included: diarrhoea, rash, candidiasis, and swollen mouth. The corresponding comparator group (no therapy) reported only one side effect of dizziness." IDSA 2019 abstract: "Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is a common finding in many populations".
claims.location: Krzyzaniak abstract (PubMed) and Results (Scite full-text excerpt); Nicolle (IDSA) abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents of aged care facilities with asymptomatic bacteriuria / antibiotics / placebo or no treatment / mortality, complications, adverse effects / trial follow-up (6 months to years for mortality)
claims.safe_wording: Many care home residents have bacteria in their urine without any infection. In trials in care homes, giving antibiotics for this cleared the bacteria more often but did not reduce deaths or complications, and caused more side effects, such as diarrhoea, rash and thrush.
claims.qualifications: Few trials per outcome and moderate risk of bias; the side-effect estimate is very imprecise, so give no multiplier. Side-effect types come from one trial only. No absolute risks available; do not invent them.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The review abstract does not report symptomatic UTI results; do not claim that antibiotics failed to prevent later symptomatic infection. PubMed abstract gives 303 participants for the adverse-effect analysis; the publisher abstract gives 317.

numbers.meaning: size of the review
relative risk of adverse effects with antibiotics, 4 trials; very imprecise; do not use in public posts

claims.claim: Treating bacteria in the urine without symptoms adds to unnecessary antibiotic use, which drives antibiotic resistance.
claims.supporting_passage: "In addition, antimicrobial treatment of ASB has been recognized as an important contributor to inappropriate antimicrobial use, which promotes emergence of antimicrobial resistance."
claims.pico_timeframe: Guideline statement; all populations
claims.safe_wording: US infectious diseases guidance says treating bacteria in the urine without symptoms is a major source of unnecessary antibiotics, which encourages resistant bacteria.
claims.qualifications: Only the IDSA abstract was read; do not quote its specific recommendations for older people.

claims.claim: Treating harmless urine bacteria increases C. difficile infection.
claims.supporting_passage: "Secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, 30-day hospital readmission, 30-day emergency department visit, discharge to post-acute care settings, Clostridioides difficile infection (formerly known as Clostridium difficile) at 30 days, and duration of hospitalization after urine testing." "A total of 2259 patients (82.7%) were treated with antibiotics for a median of 7 days (IQR, 4-9 days)." "Treatment of ASB was associated with longer duration of hospitalization after urine testing (4 vs 3 days; relative risk, 1.37; 95% CI, 1.28-1.47). No other differences in secondary outcomes were identified after propensity weighting."
claims.pico_timeframe: 2,733 hospitalised medical patients with ASB, 46 Michigan hospitals / antibiotic treatment vs none / 30-day outcomes including C. difficile
claims.safe_wording: Do not claim C. difficile as a harm of treating urine bacteria in this post; the ASB study that measured it found no difference. If useful for practitioners: in 46 US hospitals, about 83 in 100 patients with bacteria but no urinary symptoms were given antibiotics, and treatment was not linked with better outcomes.
claims.qualifications: Observational hospital study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Antibiotics in general are a known risk factor for C. difficile, but no source for that was opened in this batch.

numbers.meaning: hospital patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria who received antibiotics

claims.claim: Nursing home staff commonly use smelly or cloudy urine as a reason to diagnose urine infection.
claims.supporting_passage: Lemoine 2018: "Of 397 contacted facilities, 134 participated and informed 444 UTI episodes. Reported diagnostic criteria were burning urination (32%), malodorous urine (29%), confusion (28%), and turbid urine (19%). Twenty-one percent of diagnoses were based on erroneous criteria." Juthani-Mehta 2009 (Table 2, p. 13, via Undermind): change in character of urine was cited as a reason for suspecting UTI in 62 of 399 episodes (15.5%).
claims.pico_timeframe: Lemoine: 444 antibiotic-treated UTI episodes in 134 French nursing homes; Juthani-Mehta: 399 suspected-UTI episodes in 5 US nursing homes
claims.safe_wording: In a French survey of 444 urine infections treated in 134 nursing homes, smelly urine was one of the reasons given in about 3 in 10 cases and cloudy urine in about 2 in 10.
claims.qualifications: France, self-selected homes; the percentages are of treated episodes, not of residents.

numbers.meaning: of 444 treated UTI episodes had 'malodorous urine' reported as a diagnostic criterion
of 444 treated UTI episodes had 'turbid urine' reported as a diagnostic criterion

claims.claim: Urine smells stronger when concentrated, and some foods and medicines change its smell.
claims.supporting_passage: Only partial: "these 2 symptoms are frequently demonstrated in the presence of asymptomatic bacteriuria due to other confounding clinical conditions, such as dehydration." No source found for foods or medicines.
claims.pico_timeframe: Care home residents
claims.safe_wording: Say only that changes in urine colour or smell often have other causes, such as not drinking enough. Do not mention foods or medicines.
claims.qualifications: Expert statement, not a study finding.

claims.claim: The 2023 Cochrane review included 50 studies with 8,857 participants.
claims.supporting_passage: "For this update, 26 new studies were added, bringing the total number of included studies to 50 (8857 randomised participants)."
claims.pico_timeframe: RCTs and quasi-RCTs of cranberry products vs placebo, no treatment or other interventions; search to March 2023
claims.safe_wording: The largest review of cranberry products (Cochrane, 2023) pooled 50 trials with 8,857 people.
claims.qualifications: Only 26 of 45 placebo/control trials could be pooled for the main outcome.

numbers.meaning: included studies
randomised participants in all included studies

claims.claim: In women with recurrent UTIs, cranberry products probably reduced symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (RR 0.74, moderate certainty): about 18 in 100 vs 24 in 100.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "cranberry products probably reduced the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs (8 studies, 1555 participants: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; I² = 54%)". Summary of findings 1 (p. 6): "Symptomatic, culture-verified UTI - Women with recurrent UTI"; risk with placebo/control "243 per 1,000"; risk with any cranberry product "180 per 1,000 (134 to 241)"; "RR 0.74 (0.55 to 0.99)"; "1555 (8)"; "MODERATE 1"; footnote "1 Inconsistency: increased heterogeneity".
claims.location: Abstract; Summary of findings 1, pp. 6 to 7
claims.pico_timeframe: Women with recurrent UTI / cranberry juice, tablets or capsules / placebo, water or no treatment / symptomatic culture-verified UTI / over each trial's follow-up (commonly months to a year)
claims.safe_wording: For women who keep getting urine infections, cranberry products probably help a little: in the trials about 18 in 100 women taking cranberry had an infection, compared with about 24 in 100 without it.
claims.qualifications: Moderate certainty (downgraded for inconsistency). The confidence interval runs from about 13 to 24 in 100, so the benefit could be small. Trial follow-up varies.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Compared with antibiotics, cranberry may make little or no difference (2 studies).

numbers.meaning: assumed risk of symptomatic culture-verified UTI without cranberry, women with recurrent UTI
risk with cranberry; absolute
relative risk; 8 studies, 1,555 participants

claims.claim: In older people living in institutions, cranberry products may make little or no difference (3 studies, 1,489 participants, RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.30): about 11 in 100 with or without cranberry.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "However, there may be little or no benefit in elderly institutionalised men and women (3 studies, 1489 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.30; I² = 9%; moderate certainty evidence)". Summary of findings 1 (p. 6): "Elderly men and women in institutions"; risk with placebo/control "113 per 1,000"; risk with any cranberry product "105 per 1,000 (76 to 147)"; "RR 0.93 (0.67 to 1.30)"; "1489 (3)"; "MODERATE 2"; footnote "2 Imprecision: small studies and wide CIs". Quality of the evidence (p. 23): "was considered to be low for elderly men and women and for adults with bladder emptying issues because of imprecision and heterogeneity between studies". Implications for practice (p. 23): "The data did not support the use of cranberry products to reduce the risk of symptomatic UTIs in elderly men and women ... However, data in these latter groups are limited to small studies with considerable uncertainty around the results."
claims.location: Abstract; Summary of findings 1 p. 6; Discussion p. 23; Implications for practice p. 23
claims.pico_timeframe: Elderly institutionalised men and women / cranberry products / placebo or control / symptomatic culture-verified UTI / trial follow-up
claims.safe_wording: For older people living in care homes or other institutions, the trials did not show a clear benefit: about 11 in 100 had an infection with or without cranberry. The result is uncertain: it fits anything from about 4 fewer to about 3 more infections per 100 people.
claims.qualifications: Only 3 trials. Certainty is moderate in the abstract and Summary of findings table but described as low in the review's own Quality of the evidence text, so use 'did not show a clear benefit' or 'may make little or no difference', never 'does not work'. The group is labelled 'elderly institutionalised men and women' and may include hospital long-stay settings as well as care homes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Internal inconsistency in the review on certainty grade (moderate vs low). No evidence opened that care homes routinely give cranberry; do not assert it.

numbers.meaning: assumed risk without cranberry, elderly institutionalised men and women
risk with cranberry; absolute; CI from about 8 to 15 in 100
relative risk; 3 studies, 1,489 participants

claims.claim: Cranberry products probably reduced UTIs in children and in people susceptible after an intervention; the review's conclusion supports use in women with recurrent UTIs, children and after interventions, not in older people, people with bladder emptying problems or pregnant women.
claims.supporting_passage: "cranberry products probably reduced the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs (8 studies, 1555 participants: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; I² = 54%), in children (5 studies, 504 participants: RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.68; I² = 21%) and in people with a susceptibility to UTIs due to an intervention (6 studies, 1434 participants: RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.61; I² = 0%)." "These data support the use of cranberry products to reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs, in children, and in people susceptible to UTIs following interventions. The evidence currently available does not support its use in the elderly, patients with bladder emptying problems, or pregnant women." "The number of participants with gastrointestinal side effects probably does not differ between those taking cranberry products and those receiving a placebo or no specific treatment (10 studies, 2166 participants: RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77; I² = 0%; moderate certainty evidence)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As above, by subgroup
claims.safe_wording: The same review found cranberry products probably reduce infections in children and in people prone to infection after a bladder procedure. Its authors concluded the evidence supports cranberry for these groups and for women with repeated infections, but not for older people in institutions. Stomach side effects were probably no more common than with placebo.
claims.qualifications: Absolute figures for children and post-intervention groups were not extracted; do not give per-100 numbers for them.

numbers.meaning: children, 5 studies, 504 participants; relative
people susceptible after an intervention, 6 studies, 1,434 participants; relative

claims.claim: Care homes give cranberry juice to prevent infections.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not found
claims.safe_wording: Do not state or imply how often care homes use cranberry. The post can address the reader ('If your mother's care home suggests cranberry juice...') without claiming it is common.
claims.qualifications: No source searched successfully.

claims.claim: A randomised trial compared external (sheath/condom) catheters with indwelling catheters in 75 hospitalised men aged 40 and over who needed urine collection and did not have urinary retention.
claims.supporting_passage: "Potential subjects were male veterans aged 40 and older who were newly admitted to or currently hospitalized in the nursing home care unit or an acute medicine, neurology, or rehabilitation ward within the VAPSHCS from August 1997 through March 2001." "Patients were excluded if they had evidence, according to history or previous diagnostic studies, of urinary retention or severe bladder outlet obstruction; ... were bacteriuric; ..." "During the 3.5 years of the study, 4,241 patients were screened for eligibility; 4,144 did not qualify based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and 22 refused to participate. Of the 75 eligible consenting patients, 34 were randomized to the condom catheter group and 41 to the indwelling catheter group." "The mean age of the subjects in the two groups was similar (73.4 and 73.7)"
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospitalised men 40+ (mean age about 73), VA hospital Seattle, 1997 to 2001, no retention / condom catheter vs indwelling urethral catheter / bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI or death, and satisfaction / up to 30 days
claims.safe_wording: A US trial randomly gave 75 men in hospital (average age about 73), who needed their urine collected but could empty their bladder, either a sheath or a catheter tube into the bladder.
claims.qualifications: Small, single US veterans' hospital, late 1990s; one sheath product.

numbers.meaning: men randomised (34 sheath, 41 indwelling)
men screened
mean age in both groups

claims.claim: Adverse outcomes (bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI or death) occurred at 70 per 1,000 patient-days with sheaths and 131 per 1,000 with indwelling catheters; unadjusted difference not significant, adjusted difference significant; the composite was driven by bacteriuria.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of those in the condom catheter group, 15 (44.1%) experienced one or more adverse events (i.e., bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI, or death) during the trial, compared with 20 (48.8%) in the indwelling catheter group. The incidence of an adverse event was 70/1,000 patient-days in those with a condom catheter and 131/1,000 patient-days in those with an indwelling catheter (P=.07)." "The unadjusted HR was 1.82 (95% confidence interval (CI)=0.90–3.67) for all patients" "After adjustment for age, aMMSE score, prior UTI, and prior urethral catheterization, the incidence of an adverse study outcome was statistically significantly lower in the condom catheter group than in the indwelling catheter group. ... (HR=2.26, 95% CI=1.10–4.62) or was the same across all patients (HR=2.11, 95% CI=1.03–4.31)." "One outcome in particular—bacteriuria—which was by far the most frequent, greatly affected these results. The results would not have been substantially different if bacteriuria alone had been considered." "During the study period, 30 patients developed bacteriuria: 13 (38.2%) in the condom catheter group and 17 (41.5%) in the indwelling catheter group (Table 2). Of the six patients who died during the trial, two (5.9%) were in the condom catheter group, and four (9.8%) were in the indwelling catheter group." Bacteriuria definition: "≧10^3 colony‐forming units per mL of a single or predominant species of bacteria", with urine cultured daily.
claims.location: Results and Methods (Scite full text, pages 2 to 3)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C12-24-a; composite outcome; up to 30 days
claims.safe_wording: Per the editor's guidance: men found the sheath more comfortable, and a combined measure of problems (mostly bacteria found in the urine on daily testing) came out lower with the sheath once the researchers allowed for other differences between the groups. Without that adjustment the difference was not clear. Do not say the sheath was linked with fewer infections or deaths.
claims.qualifications: Composite outcome dominated by screen-detected bacteriuria; symptomatic infections and deaths were few and not separately significant. Similar proportions in each group had at least one event (44 in 100 vs 49 in 100). Small trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors' abstract says condom catheters are 'less likely to lead to bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI, or death'; this overstates what the data show for infections and deaths. Older observational studies cited in the paper point both ways (one Danish survey found more UTI with condom catheters).

numbers.meaning: incidence of the composite (bacteriuria, symptomatic UTI or death), sheath vs indwelling; unadjusted P=.07
men with at least one composite event, sheath vs indwelling
adjusted hazard ratio for the composite, indwelling vs sheath; relative; practitioner use only
unadjusted hazard ratio; not significant

claims.claim: Men rated sheaths as more comfortable and less painful than indwelling catheters.
claims.supporting_passage: "Based on questionnaire results, patients with a condom catheter were more likely to report their device to be comfortable (P=.02) and not painful (P=.02) than were patients with an indwelling catheter (Table 4). On other measures of preference, there were no significant differences."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C12-24-a; satisfaction questionnaire (discomfort, restriction, pain, embarrassment, inconvenience)
claims.safe_wording: Men given a sheath were more likely to say it was comfortable and not painful than men given a catheter tube.
claims.qualifications: No difference on the other measures (restriction of movement, embarrassment, inconvenience). Unblinded, as it had to be.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors note condom catheters 'tend to fall off'.

claims.claim: The difference was clearest in men without dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: "By chance, a significantly (P<.01) greater percentage of patients with dementia were assigned to the condom catheter group (60.6%) than to the indwelling group (20.5%)." "When the analysis was restricted to patients without dementia, the effect was stronger, with an HR of 4.84 (95% CI=1.46–16.02)" "Figures 1B and C show that the difference in adverse outcomes was even greater for patients without dementia (P=.01) but was not significantly different for those with dementia (P=.78)." "For men without dementia, use of a condom catheter rather than an indwelling urinary catheter appears to be highly beneficial in reducing clinically important adverse outcomes, but there may be no benefit in using a condom catheter in patients with dementia."
claims.pico_timeframe: Subgroups by dementia status; pre-specified effect modification
claims.safe_wording: In men without dementia the difference was larger; in men with dementia the trial did not show a clear difference.
claims.qualifications: Subgroup analysis in a small trial with a chance imbalance in dementia between groups. Same composite outcome (mostly bacteriuria).

numbers.meaning: proportion with dementia, sheath vs indwelling group (chance imbalance)

claims.claim: The CDC guideline suggests considering external catheters for cooperative men without urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction.
claims.supporting_passage: "B. Consider using alternatives to indwelling urethral catheterization in selected patients when appropriate. 1. Consider using external catheters as an alternative to indwelling urethral catheters in cooperative male patients without urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction. (Category II) (Key Question 2A)"
claims.location: Section II Summary of Recommendations, I.B.1 (p. 321)
claims.pico_timeframe: Male hospital patients and long-term care residents; guideline (2009)
claims.safe_wording: US infection control guidance suggests considering a sheath instead of a catheter tube for men who can cooperate and whose bladder empties (no retention or blockage).
claims.qualifications: Category II (weaker) recommendation; US, 2009.

claims.claim: Sheaths need correct sizing, secure but not tight application, daily changes and regular skin checks; complications include skin irritation, maceration, pressure damage and rarely penile ischaemia from poor sizing.
claims.supporting_passage: Hamilton 2026: "It is primarily indicated for patients with urinary incontinence who have the ability to void spontaneously but require continuous collection of urine for comfort, hygiene or skin protection. Condom catheters should be avoided for long-term use in patients with impaired sensation or high risk of skin breakdown without careful monitoring. Adverse effects are typically minor but can include skin irritation, maceration, pressure necrosis, allergic dermatitis and urinary tract infections. Rare complications include penile ischaemia, oedema and urethral injury from improper sizing or application. This article includes guidance for safe use such as appropriate sizing, secure but non-constrictive application, daily changes and regular inspection of penile skin." Saint 2006: "Although indwelling catheters generally cause discomfort, condom catheters tend to fall off, and both are associated with bacteriuria."
claims.pico_timeframe: Men using condom catheters; practical guidance
claims.safe_wording: A sheath needs the right size, fitted firmly but not tightly, changed daily, with the skin checked regularly. Problems are usually minor, such as sore or damp skin, but a badly sized sheath can rarely cut off blood flow. It suits men who can pass urine on their own.
claims.qualifications: Narrative nursing review, not a trial or national guideline; RCN guidance not opened.

claims.claim: Duration of catheterisation is the main risk factor for catheter-associated urinary tract infection; almost everyone with a catheter develops bacteria in the urine within a month.
claims.supporting_passage: epic3: "After a few days of catheterisation, microorganisms may be isolated from urine and, in the absence of any symptoms of UTI, this is called 'bacteriuria'. The duration of catheterisation is the dominant risk factor for CAUTI, and virtually all catheterised patients develop bacteriuria within 1 month." Meddings 2010 abstract: "Prolonged catheterization is the primary risk factor for catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)."
claims.location: epic3 short-term urethral catheters background (PMC full text); Meddings abstract (background)
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients with short-term indwelling urethral catheters, hospital
claims.safe_wording: The longer a catheter stays in, the higher the risk of infection; almost everyone with a catheter has bacteria in their urine within a month (UK national guidance, epic3).
claims.qualifications: Background statement in a guideline, not a new finding; bacteriuria is not the same as infection.

numbers.meaning: time by which virtually all catheterised patients develop bacteriuria

claims.claim: In hospital studies, reminders and stop orders to remove catheters cut the rate of catheter-associated UTI by about half.
claims.supporting_passage: Meddings abstract: "Only interventional studies that used reminders to physicians or nurses that a urinary catheter was in use or stop orders to prompt catheter removal in hospitalized adults were included." "The rate of CAUTI (episodes per 1000 catheter-days) was reduced by 52% (P < .001) with use of a reminder or stop order. The mean duration of catheterization decreased by 37%, resulting in 2.61 fewer days of catheterization per patient in the intervention versus control groups" "Recatheterization rates were similar in control and intervention groups." epic3: "It included 14 studies (one RCT, one NRCT, three controlled before-after studies and nine uncontrolled before-after studies)." "Many studies in this area are uncontrolled before-after designs and therefore susceptible to bias in favour of the intervention."
claims.location: Meddings abstract (Methods, Results); epic3 evidence synopsis for UC23
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospitalised adults with catheters / reminder or stop-order systems / usual care or before period / CAUTI per 1,000 catheter-days, catheter duration / during admission
claims.safe_wording: In hospital studies, simple prompts to remove catheters (reminders or automatic stop orders) about halved the rate of catheter infections and shortened catheter use by about 2.6 days per patient.
claims.qualifications: Hospital inpatients only: do not apply to discharge, care homes or home. Relative reduction (per 1,000 catheter-days); most studies were uncontrolled before-after designs, prone to overestimating benefit.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Another review summarised in epic3 found insufficient data on CAUTI for reminder interventions, though they shortened catheter duration.

numbers.meaning: relative reduction in CAUTI rate per 1,000 catheter-days, hospital studies
relative reduction in mean catheter duration; absolute fewer catheter days per patient
studies in the meta-analysis (mostly before-after)

claims.claim: UK national guidance recommends documenting the reason for a catheter, date of insertion, expected duration and planned date of removal, and reviewing the need daily.
claims.supporting_passage: "UC2 Document the clinical indication(s) for catheterisation, date of insertion, expected duration, type of catheter and drainage system, and planned date of removal. Class D/GPP" "UC3 Assess and record the reasons for catheterisation every day. Remove the catheter when no longer clinically indicated. Class D/GPP"
claims.location: epic3, Short-term indwelling urethral catheters recommendations UC2, UC3
claims.pico_timeframe: NHS hospitals in England; short-term urethral catheters; guideline 2014
claims.safe_wording: National guidance for NHS hospitals in England (epic3) says the record should state why the catheter went in, when, how long it is expected to stay and the planned date for removal, and that the need for it should be checked every day.
claims.qualifications: England, hospitals, 2014; Class D/GPP means expert opinion or good practice rather than trial evidence. Scottish guidance not checked.

claims.claim: UK guidance says no patient should be discharged or transferred with a short-term catheter without a documented plan, and patients and families should be told the reason and the plan for review and removal.
claims.supporting_passage: "UC24 No patient should be discharged or transferred with a short-term indwelling urethral catheter without a plan documenting the: New recommendation Class D/GPP" "UC22 Ensure patients, relatives and carers are given information regarding the reason for the catheter and the plan for review and removal. If discharged with a catheter, the patient should be given written information and shown how to: Class D/GPP"
claims.location: epic3, recommendations UC22 and UC24 (list items after the colon lost in the PMC text)
claims.pico_timeframe: NHS hospitals in England; discharge or transfer with a short-term urethral catheter
claims.safe_wording: The same guidance says nobody should leave hospital, or move to another ward or service, with a short-term catheter unless a plan is written down, and that the person and their family should be told why the catheter is there and when it will be reviewed and removed.
claims.qualifications: The list of items the UC24 plan must document could not be read; do not list them as epic3's words. The three fields in the post (reason, date inserted, removal or trial-without-catheter plan with who does it) are supported by UC2 plus UC22, plus Prieto's definition of an active removal plan.

claims.claim: In a UK survey, only half of people with a newly placed catheter on district nursing caseloads had a plan for its removal.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A total of 49,575 patients were included in the survey, of whom 5352 had an indwelling urinary catheter." "Of catheters, 5% were newly placed (within four weeks). Of these, most (77%) had a documented indication for insertion. Only half of patients with a newly placed catheter had a plan for its removal. This varied between organisations in the range of 20%–96%." Full text: "An active removal plan was defined as a plan that included one or more of the following: (1) a date for review of the ongoing need for the catheter; (2) a date for removal of the catheter ('trial without catheter' [TWOC]); and (3) referral to DN/urology/continence service." "Only half (134/267 [50%]) of patients had an active plan for the removal of the catheter. Patients were more likely to have an active removal plan if discharged from urology (23/34 [67%]) or A&E (11/13 [85%]; P = 0.024)." Discussion: "Given the high proportion of newly catheterised patients discharged from hospital without an active plan for removal of the catheter, the establishment of an optimal management pathway ... should be the focus of future prevention efforts."

candidates.reason: Essential claims supported from the Zisberg 2011 abstract (352 continent people aged 70+, 60 or about 1 in 6 with new self-reported incontinence at discharge; adjusted odds higher with pads and catheters) and the CDC guideline (catheters not for managing incontinence; not a substitute for nursing care). The judge's confounding concern is confirmed and supported by Larsen 2023 (severely frail patients more likely to become pad users), so the post must say sicker or frailer people are more likely to be given pads and the study shows a link, not proof of cause. The unsourced claim that records reflect products (C12-09-e) is dropped; do not assert that the 'incontinent' label drives discharge planning or care home referrals. Odds ratios must not be turned into 'times more likely'. Frame the fix (help to the toilet, answered call bells, asking about continence before admission) as the post's judgement.

Midthun 2004 supports 'wrong in about 1 in 3' only against a laboratory reference (bacteriuria), not true infection. UKHSA wording could not be opened (search extract only), so the UK guidance claim fails and must not be quoted. Important conflicting evidence: Juthani-Mehta 2009 found a change in urine colour, smell or visible blood modestly raised the chance of lab signs of infection (47 in 100 vs 31 in 100), though those lab signs are not sufficient for infection. Harms of treating bacteria without symptoms are supported by a care home systematic review (more side effects such as diarrhoea, rash and thrush; no difference in deaths or complications) and the IDSA abstract (resistance), but C. difficile is not supported (Petty 2019 found no difference) and the foods and medicines claim was not found. Cloudiness has weaker direct evidence than smell or colour.
candidates.revised_angle: Correct a named belief with honest nuance. Opening: 'Many people, including care staff, take smelly or dark urine as a sign of infection.' (French nursing homes cited smelly urine in about 3 in 10 treated infections.) Smell and colour are poor guides on their own: in a small US study judging by the smell of wet pads disagreed with urine tests about 1 time in 3, and in a larger US nursing home study a change in colour, smell or visible blood raised the chance of lab signs of infection only modestly (about 47 in 100 vs 31 in 100). Those lab signs are common in residents with no infection, and care home infection criteria look for new urinary symptoms instead: pain or burning passing urine; new or much worse urgency, frequency or leaking; pain low in the tummy or in the side; visible blood; fever with any of these. Changes in smell or colour often have other causes, such as not drinking enough. Treating bacteria without symptoms brought more side effects (diarrhoea, rash, thrush) and no clear benefit in care home trials, and adds to antibiotic resistance. Close: report new symptoms promptly, and ask whether antibiotics are being suggested for smell or colour alone. Do not cite UKHSA, do not mention C. difficile or foods and medicines, and prefer 'smell or colour' over 'cloudiness'. Visible blood belongs in the 'report' column.

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported from the Cochrane 2023 abstract and Summary of findings table (read via Undermind). Absolute numbers now available: women with recurrent UTI about 24 in 100 without cranberry vs about 18 in 100 with it (moderate certainty); older people in institutions about 11 in 100 either way (RR 0.93, 0.67 to 1.30), which fits anything from about 4 fewer to 3 more per 100. The judge's certainty question is resolved with a caveat: abstract and Summary of findings say moderate (downgraded for imprecision) but the review's own Quality of evidence text says low, so use 'did not show a clear benefit' or 'may make little or no difference'. Do not assert that care homes routinely give cranberry (not sourced). The review's conclusion supports cranberry for women with repeated infections, children and after bladder procedures; 'living at home' is an inference, so say 'women who keep getting infections'.

Full text of Saint 2006 opened. The judge's and editor's concern is confirmed verbatim: 'One outcome in particular—bacteriuria—which was by far the most frequent, greatly affected these results.' The unadjusted difference was not significant (70 vs 131 per 1,000 patient-days, P=.07; HR 1.82, 0.90 to 3.67); the adjusted was (HR 2.11, 1.03 to 4.31); similar shares of men had any event (44 vs 49 in 100). Comfort and pain results are supported. Benefit confined to men without dementia (subgroup, with a chance dementia imbalance). CDC suggests considering external catheters in cooperative men without retention or outlet obstruction (Category II). Sizing, secure but not tight fit, daily change and skin checks are supported by a 2026 UK nursing review. Wording must follow the editor: 'more comfortable, with a composite outcome driven by bacteriuria', never 'fewer infections or deaths'.

Supported by UK sources. epic3 (national guideline for NHS hospitals in England, full text via PMC) states duration is the dominant risk factor, recommends documenting indication, insertion date, expected duration and planned removal date (UC2), daily review (UC3), telling patients and families the reason and plan (UC22), and that no patient should be discharged or transferred with a short-term catheter without a documented plan (UC24). The judge's gap (no UK source on missing removal plans) is filled by the CCaMa survey (Prieto 2020): only half of 267 newly catheterised people on UK district nursing caseloads had any removal plan (review date, trial-without-catheter date, or referral to district nurses, urology or continence service), ranging from 20 to 96 in 100 between organisations; only 13 in 100 had a catheter passport. The Meddings 'about half' reduction must be presented as hospital inpatient evidence only, from mostly before-after studies. No national NHS passport verified: say 'some services use'. The UC24 bullet list could not be read, so do not quote its items.
